newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn upper house rejects part of austerity plan.
newsitem.headline: Bonn upper house rejects part of austerity plan.

text.p: The German upper house of parliament, in a widely expected move, on Thursday rejected key parts of the Bonn government's austerity package.
The opposition Social Democrat-dominated Bundesrat lodged objections to Bonn's plans to cut sick pay and workers' protection from firing and to a host of pension and health system reforms.
But Chancellor Helmut Kohl is confident that a lower house majority will overrule the upper house and pass the bills into law on Friday.

SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine criticised the controversial bills, which would account for around one third of the total 70 billion marks of public spending cuts Bonn is seeking, saying they endangered Germany's famous social consensus.
"The country needs social reform, not a dismantling of society and a scrapping of workers' rights," he told the upper house.
He said changes to sick pay rules and the reduction in workers' protection from firing would not lead to the creation of a single new job.
"All experts agree unemployment will rise again next year rather than fall. So the government's claim for its programme is false. That is why we are rejecting it," Lafontaine added.

German unemployment rose to a post-war record of four million earlier this year and is stubbornly refusing to drop back despite a recovery in economic growth. Most forecasters see it staying high next year.

While Bonn's austerity plan does contain a hefty dose of deregulation and reform aimed at promoting employment in the longer term, its immediate aim is to slash public spending in 1997 -- the year on which eligibility for the single European currency is to be judged.

Germany faces a public deficit of nearly four percent of gross domestic product this year and is desperate to cut it to under three percent in 1997 as targeted by the Maastricht Treaty on economic and monetary union.
But even if it succeeds, its total public debt level is likely to be around 62 percent of GDP next year -- above the 60 percent required by the treaty.
While the treaty allows for flexible interpretation of these "reference values", Germany may be making a rod for its own back by insisting on strict interpretation.

Of the 50 billion marks of public spending cuts and 20 billion marks of social security fund cuts Bonn is looking for, the chunk of the austerity package currently in parliament accounts mainly for the latter sum.
Other cuts of about 15 billion marrks have been achieved by a moderate public sector wage deal for next year and the government plans to axe another 20 billion from its own direct spending next year.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel is also reckoning on cuts of around 12 to 13 billion marks from the federal states.

Further hoped-for savings such as a delay in a planned rise in child benefit will have to be thrashed out in negotiations with the upper house over the 1997 tax bill which cannot simply be overriden by the lower house because it directly affects the budgets of the states who are represented in the upper house.
